value: Every pub fn added for internal use costs a grade point until it has an outside caller. hexa's own dead-export detector caught rule_error_count, covers and memory_dir in three consecutive commits this session, each dropping the score 100 -> 99. Make it private unless a consumer outside the crate needs it; run hexa analyze . before committing, not after.

docs/* is ignored with four pages un-ignored by name, so a new docs/ page is silently dropped by git add -A. The shipped-docs link test reads the filesystem, where the file exists, so it passes while a clone would have a README pointing at nothing. After adding a file under docs/, check git check-ignore -v on it.

In the TypeScript reference extractor, skipping export_statement to avoid re-reporting 'export ... from "x"' also skipped the body of every exported function, hiding a dynamic import() and a type-position import(). Skip by shape (a declaration contains no call expression) rather than by statement kind.

A grade-drop fixture that adds a function to the dirty side also adds a dead export, so the drop reads 11 rather than 10 and the test fails for a reason unrelated to its subject. Clean and dirty fixtures must differ only in the property under test.

docs/EVIDENCE.md promises every number has a command behind it, but nothing re-runs them. Three test counts were understated (8->13, 8->10, 9->10) before anyone noticed. Re-run every command on that page when touching it; a test that diffs the printed counts would make the promise self-enforcing.

hexa loop keeps a 'running' block in .hexa/loop.json when the verb that wrote it is killed. After pkill of hexa harden, hexa loop still printed 'running harden/hunt 1m10s' with a duration that kept growing, and a stage change did not clear it; only hexa loop clear did. The block records a pid, so liveness is checkable — the display should say ended or stale when that pid is gone. Same shape as the dashboard-that-lied case (analysis/2609151730).

hexa harden cannot run where no tier resolves: frontier 'claude' returned an empty reply and the local tier refused, and the run kept cycling dimensions (correctness, concurrency, durability-safety) failing each one rather than stopping at the first unavailable provider. hexa doctor reports the tiers up front; harden could check the same thing before the first hunt.

I recorded a gap saying hexa loop shows a killed verb as live. It does not: running_line_at renders 'stalled <verb>/<phase>, last seen HH:MM' once the record stops being written, with a 60s grace of two heartbeats (ADR-2609131611 §2) and a test called a_record_that_stopped_reporting_is_stalled_not_running. I looked inside the grace window and read the elapsed-since-started figure as a liveness claim. What is true: the running block stays in loop.json after a killed run until loop clear or a clean exit. Read the rendering code before writing down a defect.

I recorded that hexa harden 'cycles every hunt dimension' against a dead provider. It does not: the lenses are tokio::spawn-ed together and only their results are collected in order, so the sequential look is the reporting, not the work. The harness also already refuses to claim a clean review — verdict_line prints 'N of M lenses answered — nothing was reviewed'. What is true: each lens spends its full retry budget against a dead provider, so the run is slow and noisy. Both gaps I filed this session were overstated; read the code path before writing down a defect.

Testing hexa loop by hand, I read a stack backtrace plus 'exit=0' as a panic that swallowed its failure. Both readings were wrong: $? after a pipeline is the exit code of the last command (tail), not the binary, and the backtrace was RUST_BACKTRACE=1 in my own shell, not hexa's output. Capture the binary's status directly (out=$(cmd 2>&1); code=$?) and re-run with env -u before calling output a defect. This is the third near-miss of this kind in one session, after the two gap: entries tombstoned above. The reflex that works: reproduce under the user's conditions, not mine.

hexa analyze on a path that did not exist printed A+ 100/100 and exited 0, --grade A included, because canonicalize() fell back to the literal path and a score from zero findings is a perfect one. The '0 source files scanned' line was printed directly above the A+ and stopped nothing. Wherever a result is computed from a count of findings, check that the scan read something first: no input is not a clean result (ADR-2609221700, ADR-2609122048).

hexa adr doctor scans source and docs for ADR-<digits> and requires each to resolve, so writing an id in explanatory prose makes that file cite it. This caught me four times in one session: naming unresolved ids in EVIDENCE.md, a test fixture id in a_refusal_is_not_a_crash.rs, the ids again in the correction, and example ids in doctor.rs's own comments. Build fixture ids at run time (format!("ADR-{digits}")) and describe example ids rather than spelling them. The checker is right; prose is the thing that has to adapt.

I reported that hexa adr doctor truncates four-digit ids. It does not: it drops a match followed by a digit, so it never reports a truncated id. The truncation was in my own shell audit command, which had no such guard, and I attributed my bug to the tool. The real defect is quieter — a four-digit dangling citation is invisible, because the match is discarded rather than widened. Before claiming a tool has a defect, run the tool against a fixture that isolates it; a number my own script produced is not evidence about the tool.
